titel: Antibiotic resistance genes in agricultural soils
kurzinfo: Antibiotic resistance genes may be considered as environmental pollutants if anthropogenic emission and manipulations increase their prevalence above usually occurring background levels . The prevalence of aph(3')-IIa/nptII and aph(3')-IIIa/nptIII, frequent marker genes in plant biotechnology conferring resistance to certain aminoglycosides, was determined by Woegerbauer et al. (2015) in Austrian soils from 100 maize and potato fields not yet exposed to but eligible for GMO crop cultivation . Total soil DNA extracts were analysed by nptII/nptIII-specific TaqMan real time PCR. Of all fields, 6% were positive for nptII (median: 150 copies/g soil; range: 31-856) and 85% for nptIII (1190 copies/g soil; 13-61600). The copy-number, deduced prevalence of nptIII carriers, was 14-fold higher compared to nptII. Of the cultivable kanamycin-resistant soil bacteria, 1.8% (95% confidence interval: 0-3.3%) were positive for nptIII, none for nptII (0-0.8%). The nptII-load of the studied soils was low rendering nptII a typical candidate for environmental pollution upon anthropogenic release into these ecosystems.

titel: Zoonotic potential of foodborne isolates of Klebsiella spp.
kurzinfo: Human infections with Klebsiella have so far been primarily associated with nosocomial infections. Numerous studies now show that Klebsiella spp. are also present in the food chain and in environmental samples. The pathogen has been isolated from food-producing animals and from food products such as milk, salads, and poultry. It is therefore suspected that foodborne infections also occur.

Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is an important human infection in the EU/EEA countries and, according to EFSA, more than 21,000 acute clinical cases with 28 deaths have been reported in the last 10 years, with a tenfold increase in the total number of HEV cases reported; the majority (80%) of cases were reported in France, Germany and the UK. However, as human infections are not notifiable in all Member States and surveillance varies from country to country, the number of reported cases is not comparable and the actual number of cases may be higher. Food-borne transmissions of HEV appear to be one of the main routes in Europe; pigs and wild boar are the main source of HEV, but deer may also be infected. There is a particular risk related to the consumption of pig liver and raw meat products. Recently, HEV has been detected in shellfish and their production environment (seawater) in Italy. HEV can also enter food through faecal contamination. Outbreaks and sporadic cases have been identified in immunocompetent individuals as well as in recognised risk groups, such as those with pre-existing liver damage, immunosuppressive diseases or immunosuppressive treatments.

Lab-grown food, also known as cultured or synthetic food, encompasses a variety of products that are produced using biotechnological methods rather than traditional agricultural practices. Some examples include cultured meat, derived from animal cells grown in a controlled environment, and lab-grown vegetables and fruits produced through tissue culture techniques. While this technology holds promise in addressing food security and environmental concerns, there are potential risks associated with its development and consumption.One significant concern is related to the safety and regulatory aspects of lab-grown food. Since these products are relatively new, there is limited data on their long-term health effects. Ensuring that the growth medium and conditions are free from contaminants and pathogens is crucial to avoid health risks to consumers. Additionally, there may be unknown allergens or unintended health consequences that could arise from consuming these novel food products.In laboratories, various types of food can be grown using biotechnological methods. Some of the most notable examples include:

Cultured Meat: Also known as lab-grown meat or clean meat, this involves growing animal muscle tissue from stem cells in a controlled environment. It aims to replicate the taste, texture, and nutritional profile of traditional meat without the need for raising and slaughtering animals.
Lab-Grown Fish and Seafood: Similar to cultured meat, lab-grown fish and seafood products are produced by cultivating fish cells in vitro. This technology offers a sustainable alternative to wild-caught or farmed seafood, potentially reducing overfishing and environmental impacts associated with traditional aquaculture.
Lab-Grown Vegetables and Fruits: Tissue culture techniques can be used to propagate plants under sterile conditions, allowing for the production of uniform and disease-free plants. This method is particularly useful for propagating rare or endangered plant species and can also be applied to produce specific plant parts, such as fruits or seeds.
Algae and Microbial Cultures: Algae and certain types of microorganisms can be cultivated in laboratories for their nutritional value and potential applications in food products. Algal biomass can be processed into oils, proteins, and other valuable nutrients.
Lab-Grown Dairy Products: Researchers are exploring methods to produce dairy proteins, such as casein and whey, using microbial fermentation or bioengineering techniques. These proteins can be used as ingredients in dairy alternatives or other food products.
Alternative Protein Sources: Beyond meat and seafood, labs are also investigating other sources of protein such as insects and fungi. These organisms can be cultured and processed into protein-rich ingredients for human consumption.
Cacao and coffee : This process involves the cultivation of cacao cells, which grow, replicate and then differentiate to produce the various components needed for cocoa-based products, such as chocolate.

The Circular Economy (CE) is an approach that decouples economic activity from the consumption of finite resources, avoids waste, opposes the linear economic model of 'take-produce-consume-waste' and replaces it with an economic model based on sharing, leasing, reusing, repairing, refurbishing and recycling in an (almost) closed loop. Such a shift from a linear economy to a circular economy is expected to significantly support the achievement of the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), in particular SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production). However, the design and implementation of the circular economy requires careful consideration of the numerous trade-offs that may arise. This is a prerequisite for achieving SDG 3 (Good health and well-being).In the transition to a circular economy, it will be crucial to identify potentially emerging risks to the environment and food and feed safety in a holistic and integrated manner in order to achieve an optimal balance between opportunities, benefits and risks. It is important to ensure that food and feed safety and environmental health considerations are included at an early stage of research or policy initiatives related to recycling and the circular economy.

Very little about the slaughter of animals is digital. In the case of cattle, the animals are herded up a ramp in single file and within minutes are stunned, bled, skinned, split, and packed into fresh and frozen parts. They are then almost immediately loaded into articulated lorries for transport to supermarkets and restaurants. But even this raw, labour-intensive industry fell victim to a cyberattack. For almost three days, the global operations of JBS, the world's largest meat processor, were crippled by a ransomware attack on the company's IT systems (FT).
